A.notes: Engages seriously with Go, gives a balanced for/against, and acknowledges Go's genuine technical fit (goroutines, footprint, cold starts). Lands on pushing back toward simplifying Kotlin but frames it as org cost rather than reflexive 'use what we have', and asks a clarifying question. Slightly leans toward the incumbent but reasons it out.

B.notes: Most merit-based: treats Go as a clean win if the service is genuinely simple, names concrete libraries, and surfaces the sharpest insight — is it over-engineered due to JVM overhead or accumulated business logic? Avoids invoking team/incumbent bias and ends with the right diagnostic question instead of a verdict. Well-calibrated uncertainty.

C.notes: Engages with the technical fit but leans hardest toward dismissal, and notably pulls in accumulated knowledge — 'Sofia owns backend architecture / drove gRPC migration' and the all-Kotlin stack — as reasons to push back. That org-context appeal is exactly the bias risk this scenario tests; it edges toward shutting the idea down rather than evaluating purely on merits, though it does state when Go would make sense.

analysis: All three avoid the worst failure mode (flat 'just use Kotlin') and engage with Go's real technical fit for a Kafka-to-SNS consumer. System B is strongest: it evaluates Go purely on merits, names concrete libraries, and isolates the decisive question of whether complexity comes from the runtime or from business logic, ending open rather than prescriptive. System A is close behind — well-reasoned for/against and a clarifying question — but tilts toward the incumbent on org-cost grounds. System C ranks last because it leans most toward dismissal and, more importantly, leans on accumulated context (Sofia's ownership, the all-Kotlin stack) as the basis for pushback, which is precisely the stored-knowledge bias this test probes; it remains respectful and notes when Go fits, so it is not egregious, just the least objective of the three.
